title: Kent Johnson Is Scoring Like a Star. The Chances Say He's a Good Deal Less.
dek: Sixteen points in 15 games, a bigger role and a 7-game point streak, but the shot quality behind it is closer to ordinary.
text:
## Who he is

Kent Johnson is a 24-year-old left-shooting forward from Port Moody, British Columbia, listed at 6'0" and 175 pounds, and he has spent his whole NHL career with Columbus. The Blue Jackets took him fifth overall in 2021, out of the University of Michigan. Central Scouting's final ranking had him No. 3 among North American skaters. Luke Hughes went one pick earlier and Simon Edvinsson one pick later.

His route there was not the usual one. He played for the Trail Smoke Eaters of the BCHL, scoring 46 points in 57 games in 2018-19 and then 101 points in 52 games in 2019-20, with 41 of them goals. Our league translation (the points a player's production in one league would be worth over 82 NHL games) put the 101-point season at roughly 29 NHL points, and the 46-point season at 12. Then came one season at Michigan: 27 points (9 goals) in 26 NCAA games, worth roughly 34 points over 82 NHL games by the same method. A 34-point pace is solid for a teenager, not overwhelming, and it is close to where his NHL output has landed in most years.

Internationally he has played for Canada at the 2022 Olympics (5 points in 5 games), the 2022 World Championship (7 points in 10 games), the 2022 World Juniors (9 points in 7 games) and the 2025 World Championship (3 points in 8 games).

Before this season he had 53 goals and 138 points in 274 games. Counting the current season, he has 61 goals and 154 points in 289 games. Last year was the low point: 7 goals and 22 points in 76 games.

## How he's being talked about

The coverage has turned from a rough year to a rebound. Inside The Rink's headline on October 31 read "After A Nightmare 2025-26 Season, Kent Johnson Is Playing Well Early." CBS Sports ran "Blue Jackets' Kent Johnson: Strong start to season continues." RotoWire noted "Five points in last two games" on October 28.

That night was the high point. The New York Times headlined its game story "Blue Jackets blow an early lead, then rescue it with Kent Johnson's OT winner," and The Hockey News called it "Kent Johnson's 3 Point Night Helps Blue Jackets Overcome 3-0 Blown Lead." Columbus beat Philadelphia 4-3 in overtime that night, and Johnson had two goals and an assist.

The latest evidence is from Saturday's loss to Buffalo. Matthew Fairburn of The Athletic posted, "Kent Johnson ties the game. Sabres and Blue Jackets tied at 1." Joe Yerdon of Bleacher Report described the play: "Kent Johnson drives to the net and gets a slick pass from Monahan and bangs it past Luukkonen to make it 1-1." The Blue Jackets lost 5-2 anyway.

The tone is mostly relief and approval, with the word "nightmare" hanging over the previous season. The numbers below support part of that story and complicate the rest.

## What the season looks like

Johnson has 8 goals and 8 assists in 15 games, 16 points, which is 1.07 a game. Last season he scored 0.29 a game. Four of the points have come on the power play. Among forwards he ranks 41st of 401 in points.

He has had a 7-game point streak (4 goals, 7 assists). Over his last 10 games he has 12 points and 5 goals, against what the model expected to be 8 points and 2.8 goals.

The role is a real change. He is playing 17:49 a night, up from 13:14 last season, and he is on the ice for 79% of Columbus's power-play chances, up from 37%. Over the last 10 games his ice time rose to 18.48 minutes, nearly two minutes a game above his usual. Even with that, he ranks 92nd of 401 forwards in ice time, so he is a top-six player, not a workhorse.

The team around him is struggling. Columbus is 7-8-0 and has 45.6% of the expected goals (the quality of chances, which is a better guide to how a team is playing than the score). With Johnson on the ice at five-on-five his team has 49.55% of the expected goals, and the team does 1.62 percentage points better with him out there than without. That is a small edge, not a transformation.

## Chances versus results

This is where the 16 points need context. Johnson has 8 goals on 4.78 expected goals, so he is 3.22 goals above what the quality of his chances would predict. He is shooting 24%, against 6% last season. Our "due to cool" flag says it plainly: the chances are real, but that finishing rate rarely lasts. Over 15 games the sample is small, and one hot month can swing a shooting percentage a long way.

His own expected goals ranking is 94th of 401 among forwards, well behind his points ranking of 41st. When scoring runs ahead of chance quality like that, it usually means finishing is doing more work than process.

Where the shots come from is encouraging. Of his 52 unblocked shots, 15 came from inside 15 feet (3 goals on 2.3 expected), 20 from 15 to 30 feet (4 goals on 2.0 expected) and 17 from beyond 30 feet (1 goal on 0.5 expected). His average shot distance is 26.9 feet. His busiest area is the low slot, with 10 shots on goal and 3 goals, followed by the left circle (5 shots, 1 goal), the high slot (3 shots, 1 goal) and the crease (2 shots, 1 goal). He is getting to the net-front area, and Yerdon's description of the Sabres goal, driving to the net, fits that pattern. Still, goals have outrun expected goals in all three distance bands, which is the pattern of a hot stretch.

## How the other models see him

Evolving-Hockey's models are less kind, though they cover last season's 76 games and not the 15 this year. They have him at 0.1 wins above replacement (0.6 goals above replacement), 291st among 401 forwards with 500 or more minutes. By chance quality alone (expected wins above replacement) he was at -0.8. That is a drop from 2024-25, when he was at 1.8 wins above replacement and 3.1 by chances.

Their even-strength impact measure, which adjusts for teammates, opponents, score and zone starts, has Columbus creating 0.18 fewer expected goals per 60 minutes with him on the ice than the baseline, which sits in the bottom 6% of forwards in chance creation. His teammate quality percentile is 0.87 and his competition percentile is 0.69, so he has had good linemates and fairly tough opponents. That context cuts both ways: it excuses some of the low output but also means he has not been carried by weak competition.

The hand-tracked data from All Three Zones (Corey Sznajder) gives a more nuanced picture. Over 16 tracked games and 178.5 five-on-five minutes, 52% of his shots came off the rush, which is the 84th percentile among forwards. His zone entries are a standout: 27.23, against a league typical of 20.14 (96th percentile). But only 41% of those entries are carried in, below the typical 45%. His shot attempts (7.06 against a typical 7.8) and shots off high-danger passes (0.67 against 0.85) are below typical, while his primary shot assists (6.39 against 5.97) are above.

In skating terms, tracking data has his top speed at 22.4 mph (76th percentile) with 19 bursts over 20 mph. His hardest shot is 80.46 mph (43rd percentile). He is a quick, rush-oriented player who is not a power shooter, and his goals have come from getting to good spots, not from beating goalies with velocity.

Our own model blends this season with last and with his role, because a few weeks is too few games to trust alone. It puts him at 0.95 expected goals per 60, up from 0.69 last season but well below his own 1.07 this year, with 3.57 expected goals for per 60 on the ice and a 71% share of the on-ice goals he gets a point on. In plain terms, the model believes in a better player than last year's, not in a point-a-game one.

## What to watch

The role is the part most likely to last. Playing nearly 18 minutes with the lion's share of the power play gives him chances to produce, and ice time settles faster than scoring does. If he holds above 17 minutes and stays on the top power-play unit, a 40-to-50-point pace is more plausible than a collapse.

The finishing is the part most likely to fade. A 24% shooting rate is nearly four times last year's. If it drifts toward his career norm without his own expected goals rising, the points pace will fall quickly, and that would not mean he got worse.

Three things would change the picture: his own expected goals per 60 holding near 1.0 for another month, which would show the chance creation is real; the team's share of expected goals with him on the ice moving well above 50%; and a drop in power-play time, which would remove the base of his production. Fifteen games is a good start. It is not yet a verdict.
